claim: Atopic Dermatitis (AD) is a T cell-mediated chronic skin disease and is associated with altered skin barrier integrity.
source: Atopic Dermatitis (AD) is a T cell-mediated chronic skin disease and is associated with altered skin barrier integrity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about AD, drawing from the general understanding in the field.

claim: Infants with mutations in genes involved in tissue barrier fitness are predisposed towards inflammatory diseases.
source: Infants with mutations in genes involved in tissue barrier fitness are predisposed towards inflammatory diseases, but most do not develop or sustain the diseases, suggesting that there exist regulatory immune mechanisms to prevent aberrant inflammation.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge from clinical observations and genetic studies.

claim: Most infants with mutations in genes involved in tissue barrier fitness do not develop or sustain inflammatory diseases.
source: Infants with mutations in genes involved in tissue barrier fitness are predisposed towards inflammatory diseases, but most do not develop or sustain the diseases, suggesting that there exist regulatory immune mechanisms to prevent aberrant inflammation.
evidence: This is an observation from clinical data suggesting protective mechanisms exist.

claim: There exist regulatory immune mechanisms to prevent aberrant inflammation in infants with barrier gene mutations.
source: Infants with mutations in genes involved in tissue barrier fitness are predisposed towards inflammatory diseases, but most do not develop or sustain the diseases, suggesting that there exist regulatory immune mechanisms to prevent aberrant inflammation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most infants with barrier mutations do not develop disease.

claim: The absence of neonatal-derived IL-17 producing γδ T (Tγδ17) cells from birth resulted in spontaneous, highly penetrant AD in mice.
source: The absence of one single murine dermal cell type, the innate neonatal-derived IL-17 producing γδ T (Tγδ17) cells, from birth resulted in spontaneous, highly penetrant AD with many of the major hallmarks of human AD.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: AD in Tγδ17 cell-deficient mice exhibits many of the major hallmarks of human AD.
source: The absence of one single murine dermal cell type, the innate neonatal-derived IL-17 producing γδ T (Tγδ17) cells, from birth resulted in spontaneous, highly penetrant AD with many of the major hallmarks of human AD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing various AD features in the mouse model.

claim: In Tγδ17 cell-deficient mice, basal keratinocyte transcriptome was altered months in advance of AD induction.
source: In Tγδ17 cell-deficient mice, basal keratinocyte transcriptome was altered months in advance of AD induction.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data from basal keratinocytes at 3 and 7 weeks of age.

claim: Tγδ17 cells respond to skin commensal bacteria.
source: Tγδ17 cells respond to skin commensal bacteria and the fulminant disease in their absence was driven by skin commensal bacteria dysbiosis.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments showing Tγδ17 cell activation by commensal bacteria.

claim: The fulminant disease in Tγδ17 cell-deficient mice was driven by skin commensal bacteria dysbiosis.
source: Tγδ17 cells respond to skin commensal bacteria and the fulminant disease in their absence was driven by skin commensal bacteria dysbiosis.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome sequencing data and antibiotic treatment experiments.

claim: AD in Sox13-/- mice was characterized by highly expanded dermal αβ T clonotypes that produce type three cytokines, IL-17 and IL-22.
source: AD in this model was characterized by highly expanded dermal αβ T clonotypes that produce the type three cytokines, IL-17 and IL-22.
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data and intracellular cytokine staining.

claim: Neonatal Tγδ17 cells are innate skin regulatory T cells that are critical for skin homeostasis.
source: These results demonstrate that neonatal Tγδ17 cells are innate skin regulatory T cells that are critical for skin homeostasis, and that IL-17 has dual homeostatic and inflammatory function in the skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing disease development in their absence.

claim: IL-17 has dual homeostatic and inflammatory function in the skin.
source: These results demonstrate that neonatal Tγδ17 cells are innate skin regulatory T cells that are critical for skin homeostasis, and that IL-17 has dual homeostatic and inflammatory function in the skin.
evidence: This is inferred from the protective role of Tγδ17 cells and the inflammatory role of IL-17 in disease.

claim: The incidence of atopic dermatitis is on a steep incline in industrialized nations with estimates suggesting as high as a quarter of children affected.
source: The incidence of atopic dermatitis (AD, eczema) is on a steep incline in industrialized nations with estimates suggesting as high as a quarter of children affected (Shaw et al., 2011; Leung and Guttman-Yassky, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Dysfunction of key structural components of epidermal barrier, such as filaggrin, are contributing factors to AD onset and progression.
source: Clinical and genome wide association studies (GWAS) in humans reveal that dysfunction of key structural components of epidermal barrier, such as filaggrin, and hypersensitive type 2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-9 and IL-13) and type 3 cytokine responses (IL-17 and IL-22), are contributing factors to AD onset and progression (Irvine et al., 2011; Paternoster et al., 2015; Malhotra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and GWAS studies.

claim: Hypersensitive type 2 and type 3 cytokine responses are contributing factors to AD onset and progression.
source: Clinical and genome wide association studies (GWAS) in humans reveal that dysfunction of key structural components of epidermal barrier, such as filaggrin, and hypersensitive type 2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-9 and IL-13) and type 3 cytokine responses (IL-17 and IL-22), are contributing factors to AD onset and progression (Irvine et al., 2011; Paternoster et al., 2015; Malhotra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and GWAS studies.

claim: Aberrant skin barrier integrity and local inflammation orchestrate the activation and recruitment of type 3 cytokine producing αβ Th17/22 cells to the skin.
source: It is widely accepted that aberrant skin barrier integrity and local inflammation orchestrate the activation and recruitment of type 3 cytokine producing αβ Th17/22 cells to the skin, where they are thought to be the arbiters of the major symptoms of the disease, including visible skin damage (Koga et al., 2008; Suárez-Fariñas et al., 2013; Mirshafiey et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2015; Czarnowicki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies establishing this mechanism.

claim: Th17/22 cells are thought to be the arbiters of the major symptoms of AD, including visible skin damage.
source: It is widely accepted that aberrant skin barrier integrity and local inflammation orchestrate the activation and recruitment of type 3 cytokine producing αβ Th17/22 cells to the skin, where they are thought to be the arbiters of the major symptoms of the disease, including visible skin damage (Koga et al., 2008; Suárez-Fariñas et al., 2013; Mirshafiey et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2015; Czarnowicki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Th17/22 cells in AD.

claim: Dermal ILC2 have been shown to be critical in mobilizing type 2 cytokine responses in AD.
source: Dermal ILC2 have been shown to be critical in mobilizing type 2 cytokine responses in AD, but very little is known about the function of innate skin T cells in autoimmunity.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Very little is known about the function of innate skin T cells in autoimmunity.
source: Dermal ILC2 have been shown to be critical in mobilizing type 2 cytokine responses in AD, but very little is known about the function of innate skin T cells in autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: During the neonatal period, skin is populated by several γδTCR+ and αβTCR+ T cell subsets, whose effector functions are thymically programmed to produce IL-17.
source: During the neonatal period, skin is populated by several γδTCR+ and αβTCR+ T cell subsets, whose effector functions are thymically programmed to produce IL-17, and to a lesser extent IL-22, upon activation in tissues.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about neonatal T cell development.

claim: Tγδ17 cells expressing Vγ2TCR are exported from the thymus after birth and rapidly populate the newborn dermis.
source: Tγδ17 cells expressing Vγ2TCR (Garman TCRγ nomenclature Garman et al., 1986) are exported from the thymus after birth and rapidly populate the newborn dermis.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about Tγδ17 cell development and migration.

claim: Neonatal wave of tissue-resident lymphocytes are not generated efficiently from adult bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells.
source: These cells are part of the neonatal wave of tissue-resident lymphocytes that are not generated efficiently from adult bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells (Spidale et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are the central population of the skin immunocyte subsets and are the most dominant IL-17 producing cells upon acute skin inflammatory perturbations.
source: Studies to date have established that Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are the central population of the skin immunocyte subsets and are the most dominant IL-17 producing cells upon acute skin inflammatory perturbations (Cai et al., 2011; Naik et al., 2012; Malhotra et al., 2013; Gray et al., 2013; Riol-Blanco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are absolutely required for acute Imiquimod-induced psoriasis in adult mice.
source: Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are absolutely required for acute Imiquimod (TLR7-agonist)-induced psoriasis in adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge from psoriasis models.

claim: Humans with the loss of function allele of the IL-17R signaling component ACT1 (TRAF3IP2) are more susceptible to psoriasis.
source: Humans with the loss of function allele of the IL-17R signaling component ACT1 (TRAF3IP2) are more susceptible to psoriasis (Wang et al., 2013), but Act1-deficient mice are afflicted with spontaneous skin inflammatory diseases (Qian et al., 2004; Matsushima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a human genetic study.

claim: Act1-deficient mice are afflicted with spontaneous skin inflammatory diseases.
source: Humans with the loss of function allele of the IL-17R signaling component ACT1 (TRAF3IP2) are more susceptible to psoriasis (Wang et al., 2013), but Act1-deficient mice are afflicted with spontaneous skin inflammatory diseases (Qian et al., 2004; Matsushima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse studies.

claim: Mice that lack IL-17R on radioresistant epithelial cells develop AD in genetic background with a type 2 cytokine production bias.
source: Moreover, mice that lack IL-17R on radioresistant epithelial cells develop AD, in genetic background with a type 2 cytokine production bias (Floudas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Increases in Tγδ17 cells in patients with aberrant skin inflammation have been observed in AD.
source: Increases in Tγδ17 cells in patients with aberrant skin inflammation have been observed in AD (Cai et al., 2011; Laggner et al., 2011; Nestle et al., 2009), but accurate assessments of their contribution to human disease has lagged, in part due to challenges of isolating these cells from human tissues (Toulon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Accurate assessments of Tγδ17 cell contribution to human disease has lagged, in part due to challenges of isolating these cells from human tissues.
source: Increases in Tγδ17 cells in patients with aberrant skin inflammation have been observed in AD (Cai et al., 2011; Laggner et al., 2011; Nestle et al., 2009), but accurate assessments of their contribution to human disease has lagged, in part due to challenges of isolating these cells from human tissues (Toulon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reflects technical challenges in the field.

claim: Mice specifically lacking Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells succumb to a highly penetrant spontaneous AD that captures most characteristic disease features of human AD.
source: We show here that mice specifically lacking Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells succumb to a highly penetrant spontaneous AD that captures most characteristic disease features of human AD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Fulminant disease in Sox13-/- mice is associated with hyperactive ILC2.
source: Fulminant disease in the mice is associated with hyperactive ILC2 and requires both skin commensal bacteria (CB) and expansion of clonal αβ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased ILC2 numbers and cytokine production.

claim: Fulminant disease in Sox13-/- mice requires both skin commensal bacteria and expansion of clonal αβ T cells.
source: Fulminant disease in the mice is associated with hyperactive ILC2 and requires both skin commensal bacteria (CB) and expansion of clonal αβ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic treatment experiments and TCR sequencing data.

claim: The initial trigger for AD in Sox13-/- mice is linked to aberrant keratinocyte differentiation at young ages.
source: The initial trigger for the disease is linked to aberrant keratinocyte differentiation at young ages.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data from young basal keratinocytes.

claim: Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are essential to maintain skin homeostasis, in part by promoting normal keratinocyte barrier formation in perinatal period.
source: Thus, Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are essential to maintain skin homeostasis, in part by promoting normal keratinocyte barrier formation in perinatal period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing altered keratinocyte transcriptome and disease development.

claim: Mice lacking Sox13 have a highly selective defect in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cell development with all other hematopoietic cell types normally preserved.
source: Mice lacking Sox13 have a highly selective defect in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cell development with all other hematopoietic cell types normally preserved (Malhotra et al., 2013; Gray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing Sox13-/- mice.

claim: Innate iNKT17 cells are partially affected in the lymph nodes of Sox13-/- mice.
source: One exception is innate iNKT17 cells that are partially affected in the lymph nodes (LNs) (Malhotra et al., 2018), but these cells are rare in the skin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: iNKT17 cells are rare in the skin.
source: One exception is innate iNKT17 cells that are partially affected in the lymph nodes (LNs) (Malhotra et al., 2018), but these cells are rare in the skin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation.

claim: >90% of Sox13-/- mice maintained on a 129/Sv genetic background develop visible dermatitis around three to four months of age.
source: Incompatible with the pro-inflammatory nature of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells,>90% of Sox13-/- mice maintained on a 129/Sv genetic background (>250 mice cumulatively tracked over several years) of both sex develop visible dermatitis in the muzzle, ears, eyes and elsewhere around three to four months of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), displaying many of the hallmarks of human AD (Leung and Guttman-Yassky, 2014; Zheng et al., 2007; Fujita, 2013; Kim, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal observation of over 250 mice.

claim: Sox13-/- mice display many of the hallmarks of human AD.
source: Incompatible with the pro-inflammatory nature of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells,>90% of Sox13-/- mice maintained on a 129/Sv genetic background (>250 mice cumulatively tracked over several years) of both sex develop visible dermatitis in the muzzle, ears, eyes and elsewhere around three to four months of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), displaying many of the hallmarks of human AD (Leung and Guttman-Yassky, 2014; Zheng et al., 2007; Fujita, 2013; Kim, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to human AD characteristics.

claim: No gross developmental abnormalities were observed in 129.Sox13-/- mice for >1 year despite the development of AD-like disease.
source: Notably, while we have previously reported perinatal lethality in Sox13-deficient C57BL/6 mice, no gross developmental abnormalities were observed in 129.Sox13-/- mice for >1 year despite the development of AD-like disease.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal observation of the mice.

claim: Sox13-/- mice exhibit epidermal thickening (acanthosis).
source: Pathophysiology included epidermal thickening (acanthosis, Figure 1A, left), marked accumulation of immunocytes in skin epithelial lesions leading to eosinophilia, neutrophilia, and increases monocytes (Mo) and Mo-derived dendritic cells (DCs) in the skin (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Sox13-/- mice exhibit marked accumulation of immunocytes in skin epithelial lesions leading to eosinophilia, neutrophilia, and increases in monocytes and Mo-derived dendritic cells.
source: Pathophysiology included epidermal thickening (acanthosis, Figure 1A, left), marked accumulation of immunocytes in skin epithelial lesions leading to eosinophilia, neutrophilia, and increases monocytes (Mo) and Mo-derived dendritic cells (DCs) in the skin (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 1B-F.

claim: Sox13-/- mice exhibited aberrant, high frequency scratching behavior coincident with visible skin lesions.
source: Sox13-/- mice exhibited aberrant, high frequency scratching behavior coincident with visible skin lesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Videos 1 and 2), suggesting an enhanced itch response.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Expanded ILC2 associated with human AD is recapitulated in Sox13-/- mice.
source: In addition, expanded ILC2 (GATA3hi) associated with human AD (Kim, 2015; Salimi et al., 2013; Roediger et al., 2014), and their capacity to produce the type 2 cytokines IL-5 and/or IL-13, was recapitulated in Sox13-/- mice (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: In young Rora-/- mice lacking in ILC2 there is an increase in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells with enhanced capacity to produce type 3 cytokines.
source: Conversely, in young Rora-/- mice lacking in ILC2 (Wong et al., 2012) there is an increase in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells with enhanced capacity to produce type 3 cytokines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), suggesting a possible counter-regulation between Tγδ17 cells and ILC2.
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There is a possible counter-regulation between Tγδ17 cells and ILC2.
source: Conversely, in young Rora-/- mice lacking in ILC2 (Wong et al., 2012) there is an increase in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells with enhanced capacity to produce type 3 cytokines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), suggesting a possible counter-regulation between Tγδ17 cells and ILC2.
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal changes in Tγδ17 cells and ILC2 in different mouse models.

claim: Age-dependent increases in IgE titer are evident by 3 months of age in Sox13-/- mice, before visible signs of disease.
source: Crucially, age-dependent increases in IgE titer, evident by 3 months of age of the mice (Figure 1H), before visible signs of disease, captured one of the major symptoms of human AD.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Significant expansion of αβ T cells in the skin of Sox13-/- mice was evident starting ~3 months of age, prior to any visible skin inflammation.
source: Significant expansion of αβ T cells in the skin of Sox13-/- mice was evident starting ~3 months of age, prior to any visible skin inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis of skin T cells at different ages.

claim: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells increased in numbers up to 10-fold by 6 months of age in Sox13-/- mice.
source: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells increased in numbers up to 10-fold by 6 months of age, depending on skin sites (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cell enumeration data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CD4negCD8neg (double negative, DN) T cells accounted for 10–20% of TCRβ+ cells in the skin of both LMC and Sox13-/- mice.
source: Notably, CD4negCD8neg (double negative, DN) T cells accounted for 10–20% of TCRβ+ cells in the skin of both LMC and Sox13-/- mice, with a significant expansion observed in Sox13-/- skin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The DN subset in both healthy and AD skin consisted primarily of MAITs.
source: Utilizing the MR1/5-OP-RU tetramer, we identified that the DN subset in both healthy and AD skin consisted primarily of MAITs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The majority of αβ T cell subsets in AD were associated with enhanced capacity to produce both IL-17 and IL-22.
source: The majority of αβ T cell subsets in AD were associated with enhanced capacity to produce both IL-17 and IL-22, whereas in control mice very few CD4+ or CD8+ αβ T cells were capable of IL-17 production, and even more constrained IL-22 secretion was evident (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The frequency of Th2 cells was not altered significantly in Sox13-/- skin.
source: In contrast to the enhanced type 3 cytokine production, the frequency of Th2 cells was not altered significantly in Sox13-/- skin, although numerically they were also increased.
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data.

claim: There was an ~8 fold expansion in cellularity in dLNs of Sox13-/- mice.
source: Matching the T cell expansion in skin there was an ~8 fold expansion in cellularity in dLNs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by cell enumeration data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sox13-/- mice show greatly increased numbers of spontaneous germinal centers.
source: The trend to this increase was evident before visible skin lesions, at ~3 months of age, and was associated with greatly increased numbers of spontaneous germinal centers (GCs), typical of autoimmune disorders (Domeier et al., 2017), with aberrant GC formation (green, Figure 2F) in the T cell zone (blue, Figure 2F) and increased number of follicular T help (Tfh) cells, GC B cells and plasma cells (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2F and FACS analysis in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: A coordinate induction of the cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-23, which promote type 3 cytokine producing lymphocytes, was prominent in Sox13-/- muzzle skin.
source: A coordinate induction of the cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-23, which promote type 3 cytokine producing lymphocytes, was prominent.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: A simultaneous increase in the danger associated molecular pattern molecule IL-33 was observed in Sox13-/- muzzle skin.
source: A simultaneous increase in the danger associated molecular pattern molecule IL-33 was observed, which has been associated with skin inflammation and itch response (Salimi et al., 2013; Meephansan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR analysis and citations to studies on IL-33 function.

claim: There was a 3-fold increase in PMEL17 T cells proliferation in skin dLNs of Sox13-/- mice compared to controls.
source: We observed a 3-fold increase in PMEL17 T cells proliferation in skin dLNs of Sox13-/- mice compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: The absence of αβ T cells prevented AD development in Sox13-/-Tcrb-/- mice.
source: Finally, to demonstrate that αβ T cells are required for AD in Sox13-/- mice, skin pathology in Sox13-/-Tcrb-/- was monitored. The absence of αβ T cells prevented AD development with no visible evidence of skin inflammation and skin histology was grossly normal, including lack of epidermal hyperplasia (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: 261 genes were differentially expressed between 3 wk WT vs Sox13-/- basal keratinocytes.
source: In all, 261 genes were differentially expressed (>2 fold changes, p<0.05) between 3 wk WT vs Sox13-/- basal keratinocytes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis revealed pronounced cell apoptosis signatures and stress responses in Sox13-/- basal keratinocytes at 3 weeks.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed pronounced cell apoptosis signatures and stress responses in Sox13-/- basal keratinocytes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 7wk the difference in gene expression was muted with 50 genes differentially expressed in basal keratinocytes.
source: At 7wk the difference was muted with 50 genes differentially expressed (Figure 3A) with no significant clustering of these genes into specific biological processes, likely reflecting the resting state of basal keratinocytes in the telogen phase.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sox13 transcripts were virtually undetectable in both Sox13-/- and LMC keratinocytes.
source: Notably, Sox13 transcripts were virtually undetectable in both Sox13-/- and LMC keratinocytes, indicating that Sox13 deficiency is unlikely to cell-autonomously impact keratinocytes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Sox13 deficiency is unlikely to cell-autonomously impact keratinocytes.
source: Notably, Sox13 transcripts were virtually undetectable in both Sox13-/- and LMC keratinocytes, indicating that Sox13 deficiency is unlikely to cell-autonomously impact keratinocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Sox13 expression in keratinocytes.

claim: Expression of Blimp1 (Prdm1) was diminished in Sox13-/- basal keratinocytes at 3 weeks.
source: However, expression of several genes critical for normal differentiation of basal keratinocytes was altered at 3wk, including diminished expression of the IL-17 target Blimp1 (Prdm1) (Magnúsdóttir et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2016), Sox9 (Menzel-Severing et al., 2018), Runx1, Irf3/6, S100a11, and increased expression of Myc (Wu et al., 2015), Dlx3,Trp73 and Maf.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and citations to studies on these genes.

claim: AD in Sox13-/- mice was associated with dysbiosis of Staphylococcus and Corynebacteria.
source: As in human AD patients, AD in Sox13-/- mice was associated with dysbiosis of Staphylococcus and Corynebacteria, but with distinct kinetics (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most Sox13-/- mice showed an early bloom of Corynebacteria (C. mastitis).
source: Most Sox13-/- mice showed an early bloom of Corynebacteria (C. mastitis, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), with the expansion maintained in some mice, but for the majority returning to the LMC frequencies at 6 mo.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expansion of Staphylococcus was pronounced at the frank phase of disease but was not obvious at 3 mo in Sox13-/- mice.
source: Expansion of Staphylococcus was pronounced at the frank phase of disease but was not obvious at 3 mo.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Antibiotic treatment of Sox13-/- mice prevented AD development.
source: Regardless of regiments, the Abx Sox13-/- mice were protected from AD. All pathophysiological features of AD were absent, with resolution of acanthosis (Figure 4B), decreased serum IgE concentrations (Figure 4C), and suppression of myeloid expansion (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and FACS data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: All pathophysiological features of AD were absent in antibiotic-treated Sox13-/- mice.
source: Regardless of regiments, the Abx Sox13-/- mice were protected from AD. All pathophysiological features of AD were absent, with resolution of acanthosis (Figure 4B), decreased serum IgE concentrations (Figure 4C), and suppression of myeloid expansion (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental measurements shown in Figures 4B-J.

claim: Vγ4+ Tγδ17 cell persistence is dependent on commensal bacteria.
source: Whereas Vγ4+ Tγδ17 cell persistence is dependent on CB (Duan et al., 2010) and parallels dermal Th17 and Tc17 cells (Naik et al., 2012), Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells were not, as assessed in germ free (GF) mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citation and data from germ-free mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells persistence is not dependent on commensal bacteria.
source: Whereas Vγ4+ Tγδ17 cell persistence is dependent on CB (Duan et al., 2010) and parallels dermal Th17 and Tc17 cells (Naik et al., 2012), Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells were not, as assessed in germ free (GF) mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data from germ-free mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Constitutive Il17a transcription in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells was not suppressed by antibiotics.
source: In contrast, constitutive Il17a transcription in Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells was not suppressed by Abx (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis of Il17a-Egfp reporter mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Corynebacteria consistently stimulated copious IL-17 but not IFNγ production from Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells.
source: While Corynebacteria consistently stimulated copious IL-17 but not IFNγ, production from Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells, so did Staphyloccus species, albeit with a consistent diminution of IL-17 amounts per cell (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro stimulation experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tγδ17 activation by commensal bacteria was not T-APC contact dependent.
source: This Tγδ17 activation was not T-APC contact dependent, as similar levels of IL-17 production was elicited when CB-activated APCs were separated from Tγδ17 cells in transwells, indicating sufficiency of trans-acting factor(s) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by transwell experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IL-1 and IL-23 from activated APCs are trans activating factors for Tγδ17 effector cytokine production.
source: Transwell cultures in which Tγδ17 cells were cultured in a separate compartment from CB-APC and then blocked with Abs against the cytokines showed significantly reduced IL-17 production (Figure 5C and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Skin CD4+ T cells in Sox13-/- mice were dominated by the usage of Vβ4 TCR, starting at 3 months of age.
source: While the TCRVβ usage of dLN T cells of WT and Sox13-/- mice was indistinguishable, skin CD4+ T cells in Sox13-/- mice were dominated by the usage of Vβ4 TCR, starting at 3 months of age and reaching a plateau at ~5–6 months (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Up to 50% of CD4+ T cells in 5–6 mo Sox13-/- mice skin express Vβ4 TCR.
source: As skin inflammation progressed to overt disease (~5 mo), the frequency of Vβ4+ CD4+ T cells increased ~3 fold and in 5–6 mo Sox13-/- mice the total number of skin CD4+ T cells was more than 10-fold greater in Sox13-/- mice than WT mice, depending on the skin site, with up to 50% of these cells expressing Vβ4 TCR (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 6A–C.

claim: CD4+ αβ T cells are the major driver of AD in Sox13-/- mice.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that CD4+ αβ T cells are the major driver of AD in Sox13-/- mice and Vβ4+ CD4+ T cell expansion with enhanced IL-22 production is the primary distinguishing feature of αβ T cells in AD, dovetailing with findings in human severe AD (Czarnowicki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by CD4 depletion experiments shown in Figures 6F,G and citation to human AD studies.

claim: CD4 T cell depletion significantly improved skin inflammation in Sox13-/- mice.
source: To demonstrate that the expanded CD4+ T cells critically contribute to AD, Sox13-/- mice were treated with CD4 T cell depleting Abs starting at 3 mos of age for three mos. Skin inflammation significantly improved, including substantially reduced epidermal hyperplasia (Figure 6F,G) and amelioration of eosinophil and neutrophil infiltration (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figures 6F,G.

claim: A single, dominant clonotype (CDR3β: CASSQDSSAETLYF) was expressed on ~70% of all CD44+Vβ4+CD4+ T cells in healthy mouse skin.
source: Analyses of skin from healthy mice revealed a single, dominant clonotype (CDR3β: CASSQDSSAETLYF) expressed on ~70% of all CD44+Vβ4+CD4+ T cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by TCR deep sequencing data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: CD4+ T cells expressing the common Vβ4 clonotypes were strongly expanded in diseased Sox13-/- mice, making up >75% of Vβ4+ conventional CD4+ T cells.
source: Notably, CD4+ T cells expressing this TCR Vβ clonotype along with a related Vβ4 sequence (CDR3β: CASSPDSSAETLYF) were strongly expanded in diseased Sox13-/- mice, making up >75% of Vβ4+ conventional CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by TCR deep sequencing data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: >90% of the Vα4+ cells expressed the comVα4 chain (CALSDNTGNYKYVF) in the skin of diseased Sox13-/- mice.
source: TCRα deep sequencing of total skin CD4+ T cells confirmed that >90% of the Vα4+ cells expressed the comVα4 chain in the skin of diseased Sox13-/- mice (Figure 6I), while these clonotypes were rare in dLNs.
evidence: This is supported by TCR deep sequencing data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: ~25% of all skin CD4+ T cells in AD mice express two related TCR clonotypes composed of Vβ4Vα4.9 TCR.
source: Together, these studies reveal that ~25% of all skin CD4+ T cells in AD mice express two related TCR clonotypes composed of Vβ4Vα4.9 TCR, indicative of antigen-specific clonal expansion.
evidence: This is inferred from the TCR sequencing data showing clonotype dominance.

claim: Removal of one innate dermal T cell sentinel subset that normally populates the neonatal skin is sufficient to cause spontaneous, highly penetrant AD.
source: Here, removal of one innate dermal T cell sentinel subset that normally populates the neonatal skin is sufficient to cause spontaneous, highly penetrant AD, with many of the major hallmarks of the human disease.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by all the experimental data in the study.

claim: Early changes in basal keratinocyte transcriptome are consistent with an altered barrier formation that is likely to have linkage to commensal bacteria dysbiosis.
source: Early changes in basal keratinocyte transcriptome, well before the onset of fulminant disease, are consistent with an altered barrier formation that is likely to have linkage CB dysbiosis and the damaging immune responses that ensue.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA sequencing data and microbiome analysis.

claim: AD in Sox13-/- mice is driven by Th17 cells.
source: AD in Sox13-/- mice is driven by Th17 cells, and transfer studies using CD44hi T cells from dLNs of diseased Sox13-/- mice did result in AD-like symptoms in Sox13-/-, but not in LMC host (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the cytokine production data and T cell depletion experiments.

claim: Homeostasis-maintaining Tγδ17 cells cannot be substituted by other type 3 cytokine-polarized T cells.
source: An important implication of our findings is that homeostasis-maintaining Tγδ17 cells cannot be substituted by other type 3 cytokine-polarized T cells: loss of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells leads to expansion of Th17-like αβ T cells that are associated with inflammation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that other IL-17 producing cells cannot prevent disease in Sox13-/- mice.

claim: γδ T cells as a population have been suggested to regulate inflammation and αβ T cell responses in mucosal tissues.
source: γδ T cells as a population have been suggested to regulate inflammation and αβ T cell responses in mucosal tissues, based on dysregulated type 2 cytokine responses in the lung of Tcrd-/- mice (Zuany-Amorim et al., 1998; Lahn et al., 1999; Guo et al., 2018), spontaneous skin inflammation in Tcrd-/-:FVB background (Girardi et al., 2002), and keratitis in Tcrd-/-:B10 mice (O'Brien et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tγδ17 cells have been considered principally as an inflammatory/pathogenic cell type, required for psoriasis and EAE.
source: However, γδ T cell subset-specific function in these disease models were unknown and Tγδ17 cells have been considered principally as an inflammatory/pathogenic cell type, required for psoriasis and EAE (Sutton et al., 2009), ocular responses to C. mastitidis to protect against fungal infection (St Leger et al., 2017), and intestinal responses to Listeria (Sheridan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The homeostatic role of IL-17 in the skin was documented but the critical cell source of IL-17 was not known.
source: While the homeostatic role of IL-17 in the skin was documented (Qian et al., 2004; Matsushima et al., 2010; Floudas et al., 2017) the critical cell source of IL-17 was not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and reflects a gap in knowledge.

claim: Vγ2TCR+ Tγδ17 cells is the critical source of IL-17 necessary to prevent skin commensal bacteria dysbiosis dependent inflammation cascade.
source: We show that Vγ2TCR+ Tγδ17 cells is that source necessary to prevent the skin CB dysbiosis dependent inflammation cascade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the study.

claim: Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are the critical mediators of skin homeostasis and acute inflammation.
source: Thus, in both AD and psoriasis models, Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are the critical mediators of skin homeostasis and acute inflammation, and the Vγ4+ counterpart, and other innate IL-17 producing T cells such as DN MAITs that are present in the dermis of Sox13-/- mice, cannot functionally compensate for the loss of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing non-redundancy of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells.

claim: Vγ4+ Tγδ17 cells and other innate IL-17 producing T cells cannot functionally compensate for the loss of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells.
source: Thus, in both AD and psoriasis models, Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells are the critical mediators of skin homeostasis and acute inflammation, and the Vγ4+ counterpart, and other innate IL-17 producing T cells such as DN MAITs that are present in the dermis of Sox13-/- mice, cannot functionally compensate for the loss of Vγ2+ Tγδ17 cells.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that disease develops despite the presence of these other cells.

claim: Skin Th17 cells are absent in germ-free mice.
source: Skin Th17 cells are absent in GF mice, and their numbers are restored to the normal range in Abx Sox13-/- mice, indicating their dependence on CB.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about Th17 cell development.

claim: Skin CD8+ Tc17 cells recognize S. epidermidis-derived N-formyl methionine peptides presented by the non-classical MHC-Ib molecule H2-M3.
source: Skin CD8+ Tc17 cells recognize S. epidermidis-derived N-formyl methionine peptides presented by the non-classical MHC-Ib molecule H2-M3 (Linehan et al., 2018) and it is possible that Vβ4/Vα4 clonotypes also recognize non-conventional MHC molecules.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Tonic IL-17/22 produced by Tγδ17 cell recognitions of commensal bacteria and other skin-specific cues promote normal development of keratinocytes in postnatal mice.
source: The emerging model of AD progression is then that tonic IL-17/22 produced by Tγδ17 cell recognitions of CB and other skin-specific cues promote normal development of keratinocytes in postnatal mice.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: In the absence of Tγδ17 cell-keratinocyte crosstalk, skin commensal bacteria dysbiosis develops in conjunction with altered skin barrier.
source: In the absence of this lymphoid-epithelial crosstalk, skin CB dysbiosis develops in conjunction with altered skin barrier, driving APC activation and setting in motion aggressive activation, infiltration and expansion of type 3 cytokine producing T cells that are primarily focused on dealing with altered CB, but also result in collateral skin degradation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Damaged skin releases DAMPs, such as IL-33 that activates ILC2, which in turn promote Th2 responses.
source: In parallel, damaged skin releases DAMPs, such as IL-33 that activates ILC2, which in turn promote Th2 responses (Salimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and established knowledge about IL-33 and ILC2 function.

claim: Human inflammatory skin diseases also involve Tγδ17 cells.
source: Human inflammatory skin diseases also involve Tγδ17 cells (Laggner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: The role of early IL-17 in human neonates in skin barrier maintenance has not been investigated.
source: While type 3 cytokine producing lymphocytes have been implicated in human AD progression and maintenance, the role of early IL-17 in human neonates in skin barrier maintenance has not been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Emerging evidence for preprogrammed effector T cells in the gut and blood at the fetal stage support the possibility that human and rodents share the similar lymphoid lineage developmental blueprint to generate pre-programmed lymphoid effectors early in life.
source: Emerging evidence for preprogrammed effector T cells in the gut and blood at the fetal stage (Zhang et al., 2014; Schreurs et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019) support the possibility that human and rodents share the similar lymphoid lineage developmental blueprint to generate pre-programmed lymphoid effectors early in life.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies and represents an inference about evolutionary conservation.

claim: IL-17 blockade is being tested clinically to treat skin inflammatory disorders.
source: Clinically, IL-17 blockade is being tested to treat skin inflammatory disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice.

claim: Emerging findings of regulatory function of IL-17 in the skin raise the possibility of potential negative impacts on skin barrier function with IL-17 blockade.
source: Emerging findings of regulatory function of IL-17 in the skin raise the possibility of potential negative impacts on skin barrier function, aggravated by the emergence of IL-22 as the pathogenic effector in fulminant skin inflammatory disorders with interference of IL-17R signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.
